summary:
FieldWise is an agricultural platform that helps farmers mitigate risks and challenges. Using NASA's data (NASA POWER and NASA SMAP/MODIS), the available budget, and a user's geographical field, FieldWise generates a customized farming plan.

It addresses three main challenges:

Crop Selection: Provides multiple rotation strategies for maximum yield and sustainability by considering various factors

Irrigation Guidance: Uses satellite soil moisture deficits to recommend when to water crops and conserve scarce groundwater.

Financial Forecasting: Estimates projected earnings to help farmers plan budgets and improve profitability.

To help farmers in Pakistan, it features support in both English and Urdu. FieldWise translates complex data into practical field advisories while encouraging consultation with local agronomists.
details:
FieldWise: A NASA-Powered Smart Agricultural Planning Platform

1. What does it do, or how does it work?

FieldWise is a free planning tool that helps farmers in Pakistan compare crop-rotation options. The farmer picks their field on a satellite map and answers a few plain-language questions: current crops, farm size, water source, soil problems, priorities and budget.

FieldWise then reads a year of NASA POWER daily data for that exact spot: temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, rainfall and root-zone wetness. From it, FieldWise calculates evapotranspiration (the FAO-56 Penman–Monteith method), effective rainfall and a month-by-month water balance. It compares three strategies: the farmer’s current rotation, a water-and-soil conservation rotation, and a climate-resilient diversification rotation. Each is scored on water use, soil and nitrogen, heat resilience and cash flow, weighted by the farmer’s own priorities and budget.

For each strategy the farmer sees:

  • a 12-month calendar of when fields are bare or heat-stressed;
  • crop-by-crop sowing and harvest dates, irrigation schedules, fertiliser bags and costs;
  • why each crop was chosen, its risks, and which other crops were considered and not chosen.

Extra tools include a soil-photo screening tool, a soil-recovery guide, crop growing guides, a 16-day weather forecast with crop warnings, and a budget planner.

2. What benefits does it have?

Farmers can see the trade-offs between water saved, soil built and cash needed before they commit to a season. The advice comes with its reasoning, so a farmer or extension officer can question it instead of trusting a black box. FieldWise turns coarse satellite and climate data into dates, quantities and costs a farmer can act on. It is free, needs no account and runs in a phone browser. In our model scenarios the alternative rotations cut irrigation demand by about 13% to 30% and fill months when fields would otherwise sit bare, though these are model results and not field-measured outcomes.

3. What is the intended impact?

We want smallholders and extension officers to make more water-wise, soil-friendly rotation decisions as groundwater falls and summers get hotter. Over time that means less groundwater pumping, fewer bare and eroding months, better soil organic matter and nitrogen, and more resilient farm income. FieldWise is a planning aid. It supports farmer judgment and local agronomists and does not replace them, and it says so throughout.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Language and framework: Python, with Streamlit running entirely in the browser through stlite (WebAssembly), so there is no FieldWise server.
  • Libraries: NumPy, pandas, Plotly, Pillow and Requests for the engine and charts, plus Leaflet for the map.
  • Hosting: Render
  • NASA data used in the calculations: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 meteorology and CERES solar radiation).
  • NASA data shown on the map only: NASA GIBS imagery layers (MODIS, IMERG and SMAP), for context.
  • Other data and methods: Open-Meteo for the forecast, Esri World Imagery for the basemap, OpenStreetMap place names, and FAO methods (FAO-56 and FAO-29).
  • Hardware: FieldWise needs no special hardware. It runs on an ordinary phone or computer, and the phone camera is used for the optional soil photo.

5. How is your project creative?

Every number in FieldWise is tagged as live, modelled, reference or illustrative, and a data-sources page states which NASA datasets are used in calculations, which are only drawn on the map, and which (ECOSTRESS) are not integrated. For each crop slot it shows the alternatives it did not choose and why. Farmers can type their problems and priorities in English, or Urdu script. Irrigation figures are cross-checked against a day-by-day FAO-56 calculation, and farmers are also provided with detailed and accurate information about their irrigation and fertiliser use.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We designed for smallholders with limited connectivity, technical background and cash, so we used plain language, a guided intake and low-cost options. We wanted every output to be traceable, and the tool never gives gypsum or pesticide doses, because those depend on lab tests and local extension advice. We were open about data limits: NASA grids are about 50 km wide so one farm is not resolved, SMAP, MODIS and IMERG are not read numerically because they need an Earthdata login, and economic values are illustrative. To test uncertainty we ran the engine on 36 district-and-system scenarios with sensitivity tests, and the preferred strategy stayed the same in about 90% of runs when every crop parameter was varied by up to 20%.
